enrichment.markdown:
**Meir Schreibman / Schreiberman**

- The outside material preserves a fuller spelling variant: **Meyer Schreiberman**, alongside **Meyer Yulewitz**, as speakers and leaders of the Non-Aligned Workers’ Party during Sokółka’s community-election campaign. The meetings took place in the old synagogue and involved competing party lists, public speeches, posters, and intense debate over control of the community council. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/sokolka/sok123.html?utm_source=openai))
- No reliable external record was found giving his birth date, family relationships, emigration, wartime fate, occupation, or address. Searches under **Meir/Meyer Schreibman**, **Schreiberman**, and the Hebrew form supplied, including Yad Vashem, USHMM, JewishGen, Geni, and YIVO-oriented searches, produced no securely attributable biographical record beyond the Sokółka memorial-book material.

**Moshe Berl the tailor**

- A related Sokółka memoir identifies **Moshe Berl** as a tailor who studied Torah after work. This places him within the town’s artisan and religious-worker milieu rather than documenting him only as a political associate. The same passage describes tailoring, hat-making, and other crafts as central occupations among Sokółka’s Jewish working population. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/Sokolka/Sok097.html?utm_source=openai))
- No securely identified birth, family, migration, or Holocaust record was located for this Moshe Berl. The name is common, and records found for other Moshe Berl or Moshe Berl Rose concern different communities.

**Shmuel Hirsch the tailor**

- The memoir adds a vivid social detail: **Shmuel Hirsch**, a tailor, was remembered as deeply observant, reciting Psalms from memory and leading the congregation in communal participation. This supports the picture of religiously committed artisans who were also connected to workers’ politics. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/Sokolka/Sok097.html?utm_source=openai))
- No uniquely attributable external record was found for his family, dates, address, emigration, deportation, or fate. Searches using **Shmuel Hirsch**, **Samuel Hirsch**, **Shmuel-Hirsch**, “tailor,” and Sokółka did not produce a dependable match.

**Sokółka Jewish community and organizations**

- The broader account clarifies that the election campaign followed the German conquest during the First World War, when Jewish political and cultural activity revived. Sokółka contained competing Zionist, religious, workers’, and Bundist currents, including Young Zionists, Ha-Mercaz, Flowers of Zion, Freedom and Resurrection, the Bund, Youth Society, Ha-Mizrachi, and Poalei-Tzedek. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/sokolka/sok123.html?utm_source=openai))
- The Bund was described as anti-Zionist and anti-religious, while the religious workers’ party sought influence among observant artisans. This explains why Schreibman’s list emerged specifically as a workers’ alternative to the Bund. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/sokolka/sok123.html?utm_source=openai))
- The old synagogue functioned not only as a place of worship but also as a political meeting venue. The community struggle was understood locally as a struggle for control of the “Jewish street,” with meetings held both indoors and outdoors. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/sokolka/sok123.html?utm_source=openai))
